subject: Audit coverage question: dedicated burst pools + VPC-only workloads
messages:
From: Gina Park <gina.park@finserv.com>
To: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: Procurement <procurement@finserv.com>
Date: Mon, 5 Apr 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SOC 2 coverage for dedicated/burst pools and VPC workloads

Hi Soojin,

Thanks for the quick demo last week. Our security team is reviewing Redwood for a production integration and has two related questions we need clarified before we proceed to procurement:

1) We plan to use a combination of Redwood Dedicated (reserved pools) with occasional burst onto shared infra during peak processing windows. Does your SOC 2 Type II report (and any bridge letter) explicitly cover those ephemeral "burst" instances? In other words, will the audit scope include the shared-hosting capacity that is used transiently for our workloads when a customer is on a Dedicated plan but overflow to shared nodes occurs?

2) For certain regulated workloads we require traffic to remain inside our VPC (VPC-only private deployments). Are VPC/on-prem installations included in the standard SOC 2 report, or do you provide a separate attestation / bridge letter for VPC-only customers? If separate, what evidence do you need from our side to support issuance?

Can you confirm the audit period your 2026 report covers and whether a bridge letter is available to attest to coverage for burst/shared capacity and VPC exceptions? We are targeting go-live in June and need to close this before signature.

Appreciate a concise summary and any supporting docs.

Thanks,
Gina Park
Director, Security Operations
FinServ Bank

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
To: Gina Park <gina.park@finserv.com>
Cc: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 5 Apr 2027 11:03:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: SOC 2 coverage for dedicated/burst pools and VPC workloads

Gina — thanks for the clear questions. Short answers up front, then a quick breakdown and next steps.

Short answers:
- Our published SOC 2 Type II (attached) covers: hosted (multi-tenant) API and Dedicated reserved pools when those pools are configured as tenant-isolated (customer-dedicated instances). It does NOT automatically cover customer-managed Private VPC/on-prem deployments.
- For Dedicated customers that rely on "burst" capacity onto shared infrastructure, we can provide a scoped bridge letter that documents how the auditor included transient shared-hosting events for the audit period — but issuance depends on whether the burst model is contractually defined and whether the burst capacity contains adequate controls (tenant isolation, KV cache separation, encryption-at-rest keys, and sampling evidence).
- For VPC-only or on-prem customers we offer a bridge letter or tailored attestation that describes controls parity and exceptions; typically we require a short evidence package from the customer (network config, KMS integration notes, and a signed MLA) to finalize wording.

Details / what we need from FinServ to issue a bridge letter for burst/shared coverage:
1) Contract clause or SOW text that defines burst behavior (how and when Redwood may route overflow to shared pools).
2) Typical burst volume profile (percent of peak traffic routed to shared pools, and occurrence windows).
3) Confirmation that your workload will not require access to raw model training data or resources outside inference serving.
4) A list of the RedWood endpoints you will use (so we can map routes to audited services).

Evidence we can provide (attached stubs):
- Redwood_SOC2_TypeII_2026.pdf (audit period: 2025-09-01 to 2026-08-31)
- tenant_isolation_diagram.png (how we isolate customer state in dedicated pools)
- draft bridge_letter_draft_finserv.docx (editable draft for legal/review)

Technical note from the audit perspective (cc'ed Karthik): the auditor samples operational windows and tenant slices. If burst events are frequent and unbounded, auditors will expect sampling evidence that includes those windows; if bursts are rare and limited, we can document them in a bridge letter with auditor sign-off provided the controls were in place during the sampled period.

Next steps:
- If you send the items in the 1–4 list above, we can draft a bridge letter and get internal Legal and our auditor to review.
- If you'd like, Karthik can follow up with a short technical appendix showing the runtime controls that protect customer isolation during burst events.

I'll hold on drafting until I have the contract wording and your burst profile.

Best,
Soojin Lee
Head of Sales Operations
Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Gina Park <gina.park@finserv.com>, Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Tue, 6 Apr 2027 08:40:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: SOC 2 coverage for dedicated/burst pools and VPC workloads

Gina — quick technical follow-up as promised. Adding a couple of specifics that auditors ask for when evaluating "mixed-mode" deployments: 

1) Tenant isolation model: for Dedicated reserved pools we run per-customer process and KV namespaces with encryption keys scoped to the tenant. During burst events we route inference requests to a compatible model variant in shared pools, but requests are processed in isolated worker processes with per-request encryption-in-transit and no shared KV persistence. Attached diagram shows our mapping.

2) Sampling and logs: auditors will request traces and sampling windows for burst events (request timestamps, host ids, and process ids) for the audit period. We retain detailed runtime logs for 12 months in our internal evidence store; for bridge letter purposes we typically extract the sampled windows and provide redacted traces showing isolation controls.

3) VPC/on-prem: when customers deploy Private (VPC-only) we operate only the control plane that manages orchestration; the data plane sits in the customer's VPC and is therefore out of scope for the standard SOC 2 report. For those customers we prepare a bridge letter that maps control parity (encryption, access reviews, patching cadence) and list any exceptions that remain in the customer's responsibility matrix. We'll need your network diagram and KMS setup to confirm parity.

4) Timeline: assuming we receive your contract excerpt and burst profile this week, we can have a draft bridge letter to your security team within 5 business days and schedule an auditor checkpoint within two weeks.

Let me know what format you prefer for the sample traces (CSV vs JSON); we redact IPs by default.

—Karthik
Principal, Infra Security
Redwood Inference
